questions.stem: What is the percentage atom economy when formula weight of product is $65$ u and the sum of formula weight of reactant is $130$ u?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
Atom economy tells us what fraction of the mass of all reactants ends up in the desired product.
A higher value means less waste, which is the idea behind green chemistry.

Step 2: Key Formula:
$$\text{Atom economy} = \frac{\text{formula weight of product}}{\text{sum of formula weights of reactants}} \times 100$$

Step 3: Substitute the Values:
Formula weight of product = $65$ u.
Sum of formula weights of reactants = $130$ u.
$$\text{Atom economy} = \frac{65}{130} \times 100 = 0.5 \times 100 = 50\%$$

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
$65\%$ would need the ratio 0.65, which is not what 65/130 gives. $70\%$ and $40\%$ correspond to ratios 0.70 and 0.40, which would need product weights of 91 u and 52 u. Only the ratio 0.5 matches the data, so (D) is correct.

Final Answer:
The atom economy is $50\%$, which is option (D).
$$\boxed{\text{(D) } 50\%}$$

Quick Tip: Atom economy is the product formula weight divided by the total reactant formula weight, times 100.

questions.stem: What quantity of $\mathrm{H_2O}$ in gram is present in $0.25$ mol of it?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
One mole of a substance has a mass in grams equal to its molar mass. So the mass of any amount is moles multiplied by molar mass.

Step 2: Find the Molar Mass of Water:
$\mathrm{H_2O}$: $2 \times 1 + 16 = 18$ g per mol.

Step 3: Calculate the Mass:
$$m = n \times M = 0.25 \times 18 = 4.5\ \mathrm{g}$$

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
$0.25$ g is just the number of moles written as grams, a unit mix-up. $18$ g is the mass of one full mole, four times too large. $5.4$ g would come from using a wrong molar mass of 21.6 g per mol. So (A) is correct.

Final Answer:
0.25 mol of water has a mass of 4.5 g, which is option (A).
$$\boxed{\text{(A) } 4.5\ \mathrm{g}}$$

Quick Tip: Mass equals moles times molar mass, and the molar mass of water is 18 g per mol.

questions.stem: What is the wave number of lowest transition associated with Paschen series?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
The Paschen series is the set of lines emitted when an electron falls to the level $n_{1} = 3$ from higher levels $n_{2} = 4, 5, 6, \ldots$.
The "lowest transition" means the line with the smallest energy, hence the smallest wave number.

Step 2: Key Formula:
$$\bar{\nu} = R_{H}\left(\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}}\right)$$
The difference is smallest when $n_{2}$ is closest to $n_{1}$, so take $n_{2} = 4$.

Step 3: Calculation:
$$\bar{\nu} = R_{H}\left(\frac{1}{3^{2}} - \frac{1}{4^{2}}\right) = R_{H}\left(\frac{1}{9} - \frac{1}{16}\right) = R_{H}\left(\frac{16 - 9}{144}\right) = R_{H}\,\frac{7}{144}$$

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
$5/36$ equals $\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9}$, which is the first line of the Balmer series (3 to 2). $36/5$ and $144/7$ are reciprocals of these values, so they are not wave numbers at all. So (D) is correct.

Final Answer:
The lowest-energy Paschen line has wave number $\frac{7}{144}R_{H}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, option (D).
$$\boxed{\text{(D) } R_{H}\left(\frac{7}{144}\right)\mathrm{cm^{-1}}}$$

Quick Tip: Paschen series ends at n = 3, and its lowest-energy line is the transition from n = 4 to n = 3.

questions.stem: Which among the following molecule exhibits paramagnetism?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
Paramagnetism comes from unpaired electrons. Molecular orbital (MO) theory shows the electron count in each orbital, so we can see which molecule has an unpaired electron.

Step 2: Fill the MOs for $\mathrm{O_2}$:
$\mathrm{O_2}$ has 16 electrons. The configuration is $\sigma 1s^{2}\,\sigma^{*}1s^{2}\,\sigma 2s^{2}\,\sigma^{*}2s^{2}\,\sigma 2p_{z}^{2}\,\pi 2p_{x}^{2} = \pi 2p_{y}^{2}\,\pi^{*}2p_{x}^{1} = \pi^{*}2p_{y}^{1}$.
The two electrons in the degenerate $\pi^{*}$ orbitals stay unpaired (Hund's rule), so $\mathrm{O_2}$ is paramagnetic.

Step 3: Check the Other Options:
$\mathrm{N_2}$ (14 electrons) fills every orbital up to $\sigma 2p_{z}^{2}$ in pairs, so it is diamagnetic. $\mathrm{F_2}$ (18 electrons) has all the $\pi^{*}$ orbitals completely filled, so it is diamagnetic. $\mathrm{O_3}$ has all electrons paired in its resonance structures, so it is diamagnetic.

Step 4: Conclusion:
Only $\mathrm{O_2}$ has unpaired electrons.

Final Answer:
Oxygen is paramagnetic because of two unpaired electrons in $\pi^{*}$ orbitals, option (A).
$$\boxed{\text{(A) } \mathrm{O_2}}$$

Quick Tip: A molecule is paramagnetic if it has an unpaired electron in its molecular orbitals; draw the MO configuration.

questions.stem: Identify correct order for repulsion between electron pair present in valence shell of central atom of molecule?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
VSEPR theory says electron pairs around the central atom arrange themselves to minimise repulsion. The strength of repulsion depends on how much space each pair occupies.

Step 2: Compare the Pairs:
A lone pair (Lp) is held by only one nucleus. It spreads out more and takes more space around the central atom.
A bond pair (Bp) is shared by two nuclei, so it is pulled along the bond axis and is more compact.

Step 3: Rank the Repulsions:
Lp-Lp repulsion is strongest because both clouds are large.
Lp-Bp repulsion is in the middle.
Bp-Bp repulsion is weakest because both clouds are compact.
$$\text{Lp-Lp} > \text{Lp-Bp} > \text{Bp-Bp}$$

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
Option (A) is exactly reversed. Options (C) and (D) place Bp-Bp above or below Lp-Bp in a way that breaks the pattern; they do not follow the lone pair spreading argument. This order is also why bond angles shrink in $\mathrm{NH_3}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O}$.

Final Answer:
The correct order is Lp-Lp $>$ Lp-Bp $>$ Bp-Bp, option (B).
$$\boxed{\text{(B) Lp-Lp} > \text{Lp-Bp} > \text{Bp-Bp}}$$

Quick Tip: Lone pairs sit closer to the nucleus and spread out more, so they repel most.

questions.stem: What is the number of $sp^{3}$ hybrid carbon atoms in $\mathrm{HO(CH_2)_2CH(CH_3)_2}$?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
A carbon atom forming only single bonds uses four sigma bonds and is $sp^{3}$ hybridised. A double bond makes it $sp^{2}$ and a triple bond makes it $sp$.

Step 2: Expand the Structure:
The compound is $\mathrm{HO - CH_2 - CH_2 - CH(CH_3) - CH_3}$, that is 3-methylbutan-1-ol.

Step 3: Count the Carbons:
$\mathrm{CH_2}$ attached to OH: 4 single bonds.
Second $\mathrm{CH_2}$: 4 single bonds.
$\mathrm{CH}$ (branch carbon): 4 single bonds.
Two $\mathrm{CH_3}$ groups: 4 single bonds each.
Total carbons = 5, and all five are $sp^{3}$.

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
2, 3 or 4 would suggest some carbons have multiple bonds, but the molecule has no double or triple bond. So (D) is correct.

Final Answer:
All 5 carbon atoms are $sp^{3}$ hybridised, option (D).
$$\boxed{\text{(D) } 5}$$

Quick Tip: A carbon with four single bonds is $sp^{3}$; count every carbon in the chain.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an illustration of viscosity?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
Viscosity is the internal resistance of a liquid to flow. We should look for the option that is not related to flow resistance.

Step 2: Check Option (A):
Lubricant oils are graded by viscosity (for example SAE grades). So (A) illustrates viscosity.

Step 3: Check Option (B):
Blood viscosity changes in cardiovascular disease, and doctors use it as an indicator. So (B) illustrates viscosity.

Step 4: Check Option (C):
Soap cleans by forming micelles that trap grease and make an emulsion. This is a surface effect, not a flow resistance effect. So (C) is NOT an illustration of viscosity.

Step 5: Check Option (D):
Old window glass is thicker at the bottom because glass is a supercooled liquid and has flowed very slowly under gravity. This is a slow-flow, high-viscosity effect, so (D) illustrates viscosity.

Final Answer:
The cleansing action of soap does not illustrate viscosity, so the answer is option (C).
$$\boxed{\text{(C) Cleansing action of soap}}$$

Quick Tip: Cleansing by soap works through emulsification and micelles, not resistance to flow.

options.text: Thickening of glass panes of old buildings

questions.stem: Identify from following, the relation between standard free energy change in a reaction and equilibrium constant $K_{c}$.
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
At equilibrium the reaction quotient equals the equilibrium constant. Under standard conditions the free energy change is tied to $K_{c}$ by a logarithmic relation.

Step 2: Key Formula:
From $\Delta G = \Delta G^{\circ} + RT\ln Q$ and $\Delta G = 0$, $Q = K_{c}$ at equilibrium:
$$0 = \Delta G^{\circ} + RT\ln K_{c}$$
$$-\Delta G^{\circ} = RT\ln K_{c}$$

Step 3: Interpret:
If $K_{c} > 1$, then $\ln K_{c} > 0$ and $\Delta G^{\circ}$ is negative, so the reaction favours products. This matches common sense.

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
(A) lacks the minus sign, which would give the wrong direction. (B) and (C) put $\ln K_{c}$ or $RT$ in the denominator, but the relation is a product and not a ratio. So (D) is correct.

Final Answer:
The relation is $-\Delta G^{\circ} = RT\ln K_{c}$, option (D).
$$\boxed{\text{(D) } -\Delta G^{\circ} = RT\ln K_{c}}$$

Quick Tip: Use the standard relation delta G = minus RT ln K.

questions.stem: A gas absorbs $120$ J of heat and expands by $300 \times 10^{-6}\mathrm{m^{3}}$ against a constant external pressure of $2 \times 10^{5}\mathrm{Nm^{-2}}$. What will be the change in internal energy of the system ?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
By the first law, $\Delta U = q + w$, where $w$ is work done on the system. When the gas expands, work is done by the gas and $w$ is negative.

Step 2: Work Done by the Gas:
$$w_{\mathrm{by}} = P\,\Delta V = (2 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}})(300 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^{3}}) = 60\ \mathrm{J}$$

Step 3: Apply the First Law:
Heat absorbed $q = +120$ J and $w = -60$ J.
$$\Delta U = 120 - 60 = 60\ \mathrm{J}$$

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
180 J comes from adding the work instead of subtracting it. 120 J ignores the work done. 240 J doubles the heat. None of these respects the sign of the work, so (D) is correct.

Final Answer:
The internal energy of the gas increases by 60 J, option (D).
$$\boxed{\text{(D) } 60\ \mathrm{J}}$$

Quick Tip: Work done by the gas is P times the volume change; then use delta U = q minus w.

questions.stem: An ideal gas expands from initial volume $5\mathrm{dm^{3}}$ to $15\mathrm{dm^{3}}$ against a constant external pressure of $2$ atm. What is the work done by the gas ?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
Expansion against a constant external pressure gives $w = -P_{ext}\Delta V$. The negative sign means the system loses energy as work.

Step 2: Find the Volume Change:
$\Delta V = 15 - 5 = 10\ \mathrm{dm^{3}} = 10$ L.

Step 3: Calculate the Work:
$$w = -2\ \mathrm{atm} \times 10\ \mathrm{L} = -20\ \mathrm{L\,atm}$$
Use $1\ \mathrm{L\,atm} = 101.32$ J.
$$w = -20 \times 101.32 = -2026.4\ \mathrm{J}$$

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
$-1013.2$ J corresponds to only 10 L atm, as if the pressure were 1 atm. $-1202.6$ J and $-1101.32$ J do not match any sensible product of P, $\Delta V$ and 101.32. So (B) is correct.

Final Answer:
The work done is $-2026.4$ J, option (B).
$$\boxed{\text{(B) } -2026.4\ \mathrm{J}}$$

Quick Tip: For a constant external pressure, w = minus P times the change in volume; convert L atm to joules.

questions.stem: A weak base is $1.3\%$ dissociated in its aqueous solution. If $K_{b}$ for weak base is $1.69 \times 10^{-5}$ at $298$ K. Find the concentration of aqueous solution of weak base.
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
For a weak base with small degree of dissociation $\alpha$, the base constant is $K_{b} = C\alpha^{2}$, where $C$ is the initial concentration.

Step 2: Convert the Data:
$\alpha = 1.3\% = 0.013$, so $\alpha^{2} = 1.69 \times 10^{-4}$.

Step 3: Solve for C:
$$C = \frac{K_{b}}{\alpha^{2}} = \frac{1.69 \times 10^{-5}}{1.69 \times 10^{-4}} = 0.1\ \mathrm{M}$$

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
If $C$ were 1 M, then $\alpha = \sqrt{1.69 \times 10^{-5}} = 0.0041$, which is 0.41%. For 0.01 M, $\alpha$ would be 4.1%. For 0.001 M it would be about 13%. Only 0.1 M gives 1.3%. So (B) is correct.

Final Answer:
The concentration of the base solution is 0.1 M, option (B).
$$\boxed{\text{(B) } 0.1\ \mathrm{M}}$$

Quick Tip: Use $K_{b} = C\alpha^{2}$ for a weak base with small dissociation.

questions.stem: What is the pH of solution containing $5 \times 10^{-4}\mathrm{M\,H^{+}}$ ion?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
pH is defined as $\mathrm{pH} = -\log[\mathrm{H^{+}}]$.

Step 2: Calculation:
$$\mathrm{pH} = -\log(5 \times 10^{-4}) = -(\log 5 + \log 10^{-4})$$
$$= -(0.699 - 4) = 4 - 0.699 = 3.301$$

Step 3: Check the Other Options:
4.699 is $4 + 0.699$, a sign mistake. 5.401 and 3.725 do not come from any correct handling of the logarithm. As an estimate, $[\mathrm{H^{+}}] = 5 \times 10^{-4}$ lies between $10^{-3}$ (pH 3) and $10^{-4}$ (pH 4), so the pH must be between 3 and 4, which only 3.301 satisfies. Option (B) is correct.

Final Answer:
The pH is 3.301, option (B).
$$\boxed{\text{(B) } 3.301}$$

Quick Tip: pH is the negative log of the hydrogen ion concentration; log 5 is 0.699.

questions.stem:
Identify change in oxidation state of oxidising agent in following redox reaction.
$$\mathrm{3H_3AsO_{3(aq)} + BrO^{-}_{3(aq)} \longrightarrow Br^{-}_{(aq)} + 3H_3AsO_{4(aq)}}$$
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
An oxidising agent gains electrons, so its oxidation number goes down. We find which species is reduced.

Step 2: Oxidation Numbers:
In $\mathrm{H_3AsO_3}$: $3 + x - 6 = 0$, so As is $+3$. In $\mathrm{H_3AsO_4}$: $3 + x - 8 = 0$, so As is $+5$. Arsenic is oxidised.
In $\mathrm{BrO_3^{-}}$: $x - 6 = -1$, so Br is $+5$. In $\mathrm{Br^{-}}$, Br is $-1$. Bromine is reduced.

Step 3: Identify the Oxidising Agent:
Bromate, $\mathrm{BrO_3^{-}}$, is the oxidising agent because it takes electrons from arsenious acid. Its oxidation state changes from $+5$ to $-1$.

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
(C) $+3$ to $+5$ is the change for arsenic, the reducing agent. (A) and (D) have the wrong direction or wrong values. So (B) is correct.

Final Answer:
The oxidising agent is bromate and Br goes from +5 to -1, option (B).
$$\boxed{\text{(B) } +5 \text{ to } -1}$$

Quick Tip: The oxidising agent is reduced; find the oxidation number of bromine before and after.

questions.stem: Which element from following forms superoxide with oxygen?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
On burning in excess oxygen, alkali metals give different oxides depending on the size of the cation. Lithium gives the normal oxide, sodium gives mainly the peroxide, and K, Rb and Cs give superoxides ($\mathrm{MO_2}$).

Step 2: Why Size Matters:
The superoxide ion $\mathrm{O_2^{-}}$ is large. A large, weakly polarising cation such as $\mathrm{K^{+}}$ stabilises it through high lattice energy.

Step 3: Check Each Option:
Sodium: forms $\mathrm{Na_2O_2}$ (peroxide) mainly.
Potassium: forms $\mathrm{KO_2}$ (superoxide).
Lithium: forms $\mathrm{Li_2O}$ (normal oxide).
Magnesium: forms $\mathrm{MgO}$ (normal oxide).

Step 4: Conclusion:
Potassium is the only element in the list that forms a superoxide.

Final Answer:
Potassium forms the superoxide $\mathrm{KO_2}$, option (B).
$$\boxed{\text{(B) Potassium}}$$

Quick Tip: Larger alkali metal cations (K, Rb, Cs) stabilise the large superoxide ion.

questions.stem: What is the number of chiral carbon atoms in 2-chlorobutane?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
A carbon is chiral if it is bonded to four different atoms or groups.

Step 2: Write the Structure:
2-chlorobutane is $\mathrm{CH_3 - CH(Cl) - CH_2 - CH_3}$.

Step 3: Test Each Carbon:
C1 ($\mathrm{CH_3}$): has three H atoms, so it is not chiral.
C2: has H, Cl, $\mathrm{CH_3}$ and $\mathrm{C_2H_5}$, four different groups, so it is chiral.
C3 ($\mathrm{CH_2}$): has two H atoms, so it is not chiral.
C4 ($\mathrm{CH_3}$): three H atoms, so it is not chiral.

Step 4: Conclusion:
Only C2 is a stereocentre, so the molecule has 1 chiral carbon and exists as a pair of enantiomers.

Final Answer:
There is exactly one chiral carbon, option (D).
$$\boxed{\text{(D) } 1}$$

Quick Tip: A chiral carbon has four different groups attached; check each carbon of $\mathrm{CH_3CHClCH_2CH_3}$.

questions.stem: Identify the aldehyde from following so that the aldehydic group is NOT attached with any $sp^{3}$ hybrid 'c' atom.
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
In an aldehyde the $-\mathrm{CHO}$ group is attached to either an alkyl group or to hydrogen. We want the one where it is not attached to any $sp^{3}$ carbon.

Step 2: Check the Options:
Methanal, $\mathrm{HCHO}$: CHO is attached to two hydrogens and no carbon at all. This matches.
Ethanal, $\mathrm{CH_3CHO}$: CHO attached to a $\mathrm{CH_3}$ carbon, which is $sp^{3}$.
2-Methylpropanal: CHO attached to the $sp^{3}$ CH carbon.
Propanal, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO}$: CHO attached to an $sp^{3}$ $\mathrm{CH_2}$ carbon.

Step 3: Conclusion:
Only methanal is not bonded to an $sp^{3}$ carbon, so (A) is correct.

Final Answer:
Methanal is the only aldehyde with no alkyl carbon next to CHO, option (A).
$$\boxed{\text{(A) Methanal}}$$

Quick Tip: Only formaldehyde has the CHO group attached to hydrogen instead of a carbon.

questions.stem: Which from following is a primary benzylic alcohol?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
In a benzylic alcohol the $-\mathrm{OH}$ is on an $sp^{3}$ carbon directly attached to an aromatic ring. It is primary if that carbon is bonded to only one other carbon (the ring).

Step 2: Check (A):
$\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2OH}$ is benzyl alcohol. The carbinol carbon is attached to the ring, two H and OH, so it is primary and benzylic.

Step 3: Check (B):
$\mathrm{C_6H_5CH(OH)CH_3}$ is benzylic but the carbinol carbon bonds to two carbons, so it is secondary.

Step 4: Check (C) and (D):
(C) is a secondary allylic alcohol. (D) is allyl alcohol, a primary allylic alcohol. Neither has a benzene ring, so they are not benzylic.

Final Answer:
Benzyl alcohol is the primary benzylic alcohol, option (A).
$$\boxed{\text{(A) } \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2OH}}$$

Quick Tip: A benzylic alcohol has OH on a carbon attached to a benzene ring; primary means that carbon has only one other carbon.

questions.stem: Which from the following aldehydes contains two $-\mathrm{CHO}$ groups in a molecule?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
We need the common-name aldehyde whose structure carries two $-\mathrm{CHO}$ groups.

Step 2: Check Each Option:
Acrolein (propenal): $\mathrm{CH_2 = CH - CHO}$, one CHO group.
o-Tolualdehyde: 2-methylbenzaldehyde, one CHO group on the ring.
Phthaldehyde: benzene-1,2-dicarbaldehyde, $\mathrm{C_6H_4(CHO)_2}$, two CHO groups.
Butyraldehyde (butanal): $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CHO}$, one CHO group.

Step 3: Conclusion:
Only phthaldehyde contains two aldehyde groups.

Final Answer:
Phthaldehyde has two CHO groups, option (C).
$$\boxed{\text{(C) Phthaldehyde}}$$

Quick Tip: Phthaldehyde is benzene-1,2-dicarbaldehyde, so it has two CHO groups.

questions.stem: Gold crystallizes as fcc unit cell, the edge length of unit cell is $408$ pm. What is the radius of gold atom?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
In a face-centred cubic cell, the atoms touch along the face diagonal. Its length is $\sqrt{2}\,a$, and it equals four atomic radii.

Step 2: Key Formula:
$$\sqrt{2}\,a = 4r \Rightarrow r = \frac{\sqrt{2}\,a}{4} = \frac{a}{2\sqrt{2}}$$

Step 3: Calculation:
$$r = \frac{1.414 \times 408}{4} = \frac{576.9}{4} = 144.2\ \mathrm{pm}$$

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
The other values do not come from the fcc relation. Using the bcc relation $r = \sqrt{3}a/4$ would give 176.6 pm, which is close to (D) but belongs to a different lattice. (C) is correct.

Final Answer:
The radius of the gold atom is 144.2 pm, option (C).
$$\boxed{\text{(C) } 144.2\ \mathrm{pm}}$$

Quick Tip: In an fcc cell atoms touch along the face diagonal, so a = 2 root 2 times r.

questions.stem: What is the number of tetrahedral voids present in $0.5$ mole of compound forming hcp structure?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
In close packing (hcp or ccp) with $N$ atoms, there are $N$ octahedral voids and $2N$ tetrahedral voids.

Step 2: Number of Atoms:
$0.5$ mol of atoms $= 0.5 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 3.011 \times 10^{23}$ atoms.

Step 3: Number of Tetrahedral Voids:
$$2N = 2 \times 3.011 \times 10^{23} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}$$

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
$3.011 \times 10^{23}$ would be the number of atoms or octahedral voids. The other values do not match any simple multiple of $N$. So (D) is correct.

Final Answer:
The number of tetrahedral voids is $6.022 \times 10^{23}$, option (D).
$$\boxed{\text{(D) } 6.022 \times 10^{23}}$$

Quick Tip: An hcp lattice has 2 tetrahedral voids per atom, so find the number of atoms first.

questions.stem: Which among the following pairs of solutions is isotonic in nature?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
Isotonic solutions have the same osmotic pressure at the same temperature. Osmotic pressure depends on the effective number of particles: $\pi = iCRT$.

Step 2: Find the Particle Concentration:
0.1 M urea: non-electrolyte, $i = 1$, effective 0.1 M.
0.1 M sucrose: non-electrolyte, $i = 1$, effective 0.1 M.
0.1 M KCl: $i \approx 2$, effective about 0.2 M.
0.1 M $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$: $i \approx 3$, effective about 0.3 M.

Step 3: Match the Pairs:
Urea and sucrose both give 0.1 M of particles, so their osmotic pressures are equal. Every other pair has different effective concentrations: urea and KCl (0.1 and 0.2), sucrose and KCl (0.1 and 0.2), KCl and $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ (0.2 and 0.3).

Final Answer:
Urea and sucrose at 0.1 M each are isotonic, option (A).
$$\boxed{\text{(A) 0.1 M urea and 0.1 M sucrose}}$$

Quick Tip: Isotonic solutions have equal osmotic pressure, which depends on the total particle concentration.

questions.stem: A solution of non volatile solute has boiling point elevation $0.70$ K if $K_{b}$ for the solvent is $2.44\mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}$. What is the molality of the solution?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
The elevation in boiling point of a dilute solution of a non-volatile solute is proportional to its molality: $\Delta T_{b} = K_{b}\,m$.

Step 2: Rearrange:
$$m = \frac{\Delta T_{b}}{K_{b}}$$

Step 3: Substitute:
$$m = \frac{0.70}{2.44} = 0.2869 \approx 0.286\ \mathrm{m}$$

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
3.48 m is $2.44/0.70$, the ratio inverted. 2.86 m is ten times too large, a decimal slip. 0.0186 m does not match the formula. Option (C) is correct.

Final Answer:
The molality is 0.286 m, option (C).
$$\boxed{\text{(C) } 0.286\ \mathrm{m}}$$

Quick Tip: Use delta Tb = Kb times molality.

questions.stem: van't Hoff factor for $\mathrm{BaCl_2}$ is $2.47$, calculate the percentage dissociation of in its aqueous solution.
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
The van't Hoff factor relates to degree of dissociation. For $\mathrm{BaCl_2 \rightarrow Ba^{2+} + 2Cl^{-}}$, one formula unit gives $n = 3$ particles.

Step 2: Key Formula:
$$i = 1 + (n - 1)\alpha = 1 + 2\alpha$$

Step 3: Calculation:
$$2.47 = 1 + 2\alpha \Rightarrow \alpha = \frac{1.47}{2} = 0.735$$
Percentage dissociation $= 0.735 \times 100 = 73.5\%$.

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
25.6%, 35.7% and 13.6% would give i of 1.51, 1.71 and 1.27. None of these equals 2.47. So (C) is correct.

Final Answer:
$\mathrm{BaCl_2}$ is 73.5% dissociated, option (C).
$$\boxed{\text{(C) } 73.5\%}$$

Quick Tip: For $\mathrm{BaCl_2}$, i = 1 + 2 alpha since each formula unit gives three ions.

questions.stem: What is number of moles of electron passed when a current of $2$ Amp flows through solution of electrolyte for $10$ minutes?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
One mole of electrons carries a charge of 1 faraday, $F = 96500$ C.

Step 2: Find the Charge:
$t = 10 \times 60 = 600$ s.
$$Q = It = 2 \times 600 = 1200\ \mathrm{C}$$

Step 3: Moles of Electrons:
$$n = \frac{Q}{F} = \frac{1200}{96500} = 1.243 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol}$$

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
$1.784 \times 10^{-2}$ would need 1722 C, $2.022 \times 10^{-2}$ would need 1951 C, $8.041 \times 10^{-2}$ would need 7760 C. None matches 1200 C. So (B) is correct.

Final Answer:
About $1.243 \times 10^{-2}$ mol of electrons pass, option (B).
$$\boxed{\text{(B) } 1.243 \times 10^{-2}}$$

Quick Tip: Charge = current times time; divide by the Faraday constant.

questions.stem: What is the conductivity of $0.02\mathrm{M\,AgNO_3}$ solution having cell constant $1.2\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and resistance $95.0$ ohms ?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
The conductivity $\kappa$ of a solution is the cell constant $G^{*}$ times the conductance, and conductance is $1/R$.

Step 2: Key Formula:
$$\kappa = \frac{G^{*}}{R}$$

Step 3: Calculation:
$$\kappa = \frac{1.2\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}}{95.0\ \Omega} = 1.263 \times 10^{-2}\ \Omega^{-1}\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$$

Step 4: Check the Other Options:
Multiplying instead of dividing would give 114, a huge number. The other options (1.140, 1.340, 1.463 times $10^{-2}$) correspond to R values of 105, 89.6 and 82, none of them 95.0 ohm. So (B) is correct.

Final Answer:
The conductivity is $1.263 \times 10^{-2}\ \Omega^{-1}\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, option (B).
$$\boxed{\text{(B) } 1.263 \times 10^{-2}\ \Omega^{-1}\mathrm{cm^{-1}}}$$

Quick Tip: Conductivity is the cell constant divided by resistance.

questions.stem: During the electrolysis of aqueous NaCl the product formed at cathode is?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
In electrolysis of an aqueous salt, water competes with the ions. At the cathode, the species that is reduced most easily (higher reduction potential) wins.
Step 2: Possible Cathode Reactions:
$\mathrm{Na^{+} + e^{-} \rightarrow Na}$ has $E^\circ = -2.71$ V.
$\mathrm{2H_2O + 2e^{-} \rightarrow H_2 + 2OH^{-}}$ has $E^\circ = -0.83$ V.
The water reaction has the less negative potential, so it occurs.
Step 3: Product at the Cathode:
Hydrogen gas bubbles out of the cathode, and the solution near it becomes basic because of $\mathrm{OH^{-}}$ (this is the basis of the chlor-alkali process).
Step 4: Check the Other Options:
$\mathrm{Cl_2}$ forms at the anode, not the cathode. $\mathrm{O_2}$ is an anode product of water oxidation, and it is not formed at the cathode. Sodium metal is not deposited because $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ is harder to reduce than water. So (D) is correct.
Final Answer:
Hydrogen gas is evolved at the cathode, option (D).
(D) $\mathrm{H_{2(g)}}$
Quick Tip: Water is reduced more easily than $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$, so hydrogen gas forms at the cathode.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an elementary reaction ?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
An elementary reaction occurs in one step, with the collision of at most three species. Complex reactions have several steps.
Step 2: Check Option (A):
$\mathrm{O_3 \rightarrow O_2 + O}$ involves a single molecule breaking into two pieces in one step. This is a unimolecular elementary reaction.
Step 3: Check the Other Options:
$\mathrm{2NO_2Cl \rightarrow 2NO_2 + Cl_2}$ is known to occur in two steps (slow step produces $\mathrm{NO_2 + Cl}$), so it is complex.
$\mathrm{2NO_2 + F_2 \rightarrow 2NO_2F}$ is known to occur in two steps through $\mathrm{NO_2F}$ and F atoms.
$\mathrm{2NO + Cl_2 \rightarrow 2NOCl}$ has three reacting molecules, and its mechanism involves an intermediate $\mathrm{NOCl_2}$, so it is not a single step.
Step 4: Conclusion:
The decomposition of ozone as written is the elementary step.
Final Answer:
Option (A) is a single-step unimolecular process.
(A) $\mathrm{O_{3(g)} \rightarrow O_{2(g)} + O_{(g)}}$
Quick Tip: An elementary reaction occurs in a single step; its molecularity is small and equals the number of reacting species.

questions.stem: A first order reaction take $30$ minutes for $75\%$ decomposition, calculate its rate constant ?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
For a first-order reaction, $k = \frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{[A]_0}{[A]}$.
Step 2: Set Up the Data:
75% has decomposed, so 25% remains. If $[A]_0 = 100$, then $[A] = 25$ and the ratio is 4.
$t = 30$ min.
Step 3: Calculation:
$$k = \frac{2.303}{30}\log 4 = \frac{2.303 \times 0.6021}{30} = \frac{1.3866}{30} = 0.0462\ \mathrm{min^{-1}} \approx 0.0463\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$$
Step 4: Check the Other Options:
0.0238 and 0.0715 and 0.0957 $\mathrm{min^{-1}}$ do not satisfy $kt = \ln 4 = 1.386$ for $t = 30$ min. For 0.0463, $kt = 1.389$, which matches. So (B) is correct.
Final Answer:
The rate constant is $0.0463\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$, option (B).
(B) $0.0463\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$
Quick Tip: Use $k = \frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{a}{a - x}$; 75% decomposition leaves 25 percent.

questions.stem: Rate constant of decomposition of hydrogen peroxide is $0.0204\ \mathrm{minutes^{-1}}$, calculate half life of reaction.
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
The decomposition of hydrogen peroxide is first order, and the half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on concentration.
Step 2: Key Formula:
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k}$$
Step 3: Calculation:
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{0.0204\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}} = 33.97\ \mathrm{min}$$
Step 4: Check the Other Options:
17.56 min would need $k = 0.0395$, 51.50 min would need $k = 0.01346$, and 68.70 min would need $k = 0.0101$. Since the given $k$ is 0.0204, only 33.97 min is consistent. Option (B) is correct.
Final Answer:
The half-life is 33.97 min, option (B).
(B) 33.97 min
Quick Tip: For a first-order reaction $t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k}$.

questions.stem: Which of the following properties of colloid is used to measure the rate of migration of sol particles?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
Sol particles carry an electric charge. In an electric field they move toward the oppositely charged electrode, and the speed of this movement can be measured.
Step 2: Check Each Property:
Tyndall effect: scattering of light by colloidal particles, used to detect them.
Brownian motion: random zig-zag motion caused by solvent molecules hitting the particles; it keeps the sol stable.
Electrophoresis: movement of sol particles under an applied electric field, whose rate can be measured.
Electroosmosis: movement of the dispersion medium, not the particles, under the field.
Step 3: Conclusion:
The rate of migration of the sol particles is measured through electrophoresis.
Final Answer:
Electrophoresis measures the migration of charged sol particles, option (C).
(C) Electrophoresis
Quick Tip: Electrophoresis is the movement of charged sol particles in an electric field.

questions.stem: Which among the following oxoacids of chlorine exhibits $+3$ oxidation state of chlorine?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
In oxoacids, H is $+1$ and O is $-2$. The sum of oxidation numbers is zero, so we can solve for Cl.
Step 2: Calculate for Each Acid:
$\mathrm{HClO}$: $1 + x - 2 = 0$, so $x = +1$.
$\mathrm{HClO_2}$: $1 + x - 4 = 0$, so $x = +3$.
$\mathrm{HClO_3}$: $1 + x - 6 = 0$, so $x = +5$.
$\mathrm{HClO_4}$: $1 + x - 8 = 0$, so $x = +7$.
Step 3: Conclusion:
Chlorous acid, $\mathrm{HClO_2}$, has chlorine in the $+3$ state. So (B) is correct, and the others are hypochlorous (+1), chloric (+5) and perchloric (+7) acids.
Final Answer:
$\mathrm{HClO_2}$ shows the +3 state, option (B).
(B) $\mathrm{HClO_2}$
Quick Tip: Calculate the oxidation number of Cl in $\mathrm{HClO}$, $\mathrm{HClO_2}$, $\mathrm{HClO_3}$ and $\mathrm{HClO_4}$.

questions.stem: Identify general electronic configuration exhibited by $2^{\mathrm{nd}}$ series of transition elements.
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
The second transition series (Y to Cd) fills the $4d$ subshell. The core before it is krypton, $[\mathrm{Kr}]$.
Step 2: Write the Configuration:
The 5s orbital holds 0 to 2 electrons, because some elements such as Pd ($4d^{10}5s^{0}$) and Ag ($4d^{10}5s^{1}$) are exceptions.
$$[\mathrm{Kr}]\,4d^{1-10}\,5s^{0-2}$$
Step 3: Check the Other Options:
Options (A) and (C) place $4s^{2}$ after the 4d, which is wrong because the 4s subshell is already filled in the core. (C) also uses [Xe] as the core, which belongs to the third series, and (D) with [Rn] and 6s belongs to the 6th period. Only (B) is the right pattern.
Final Answer:
The 4d series has the configuration $[\mathrm{Kr}]\,4d^{1-10}5s^{0-2}$, option (B).
(B) $[\mathrm{Kr}]\,4d^{1-10}\,5s^{0-2}$
Quick Tip: The second series fills 4d with 5s outer electrons, after krypton.

questions.stem: Identify metals present in brass.
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements. Common alloys are tested often in the d-block chapter.
Step 2: Composition of Brass:
Brass is about 60-80% copper and 20-40% zinc.
Step 3: Compare the Options:
Ni and Cu: this pairing is found in the alloy called cupronickel (coins).
Fe and Zn: not a standard alloy pair.
Cr and Sn: not a standard alloy pair either.
Cu and Zn: brass.
Step 4: Conclusion:
The metals in brass are copper and zinc, option (D).
Final Answer:
Brass contains Cu and Zn, option (D).
(D) Cu and Zn
Quick Tip: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.

questions.stem: What is the highest possible oxidation state exhibited by manganese ?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
The highest oxidation state of a 3d element is usually the sum of its $4s$ and $3d$ electrons.
Step 2: Manganese:
Mn has the configuration $[\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{2}$, which has 7 valence electrons. Removing all of them gives $+7$, as in $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ and $\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}$.
Step 3: Check the Other Options:
$+8$ is not possible because there are only 7 electrons available. $+5$ and $+6$ are real states (manganate(V) and manganate(VI) ions), but they are not the highest. So (D) is correct.
Final Answer:
The highest oxidation state of Mn is +7, option (D).
(D) $+7$
Quick Tip: Manganese uses all 7 valence electrons ($3d^{5}4s^{2}$) to show +7.

questions.stem: What type of hybridization is found in $\mathrm{[Ni(Cl)_4]^{2-}}$?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
The hybridisation of a complex depends on the metal electron configuration and the strength of the ligand field.
Step 2: Find the Oxidation State:
In $\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}$, $x - 4 = -2$, so Ni is $+2$ and has the configuration $3d^{8}$.
Step 3: Ligand Field:
Chloride is a weak field ligand. It does not force the d electrons to pair, so the 3d orbitals stay occupied and the 4s and 4p orbitals are used.
Step 4: Hybridisation:
One 4s and three 4p orbitals mix to give four $sp^{3}$ orbitals, so the shape is tetrahedral and the complex is paramagnetic with two unpaired electrons.
A $dsp^{2}$ square planar shape would need strong field ligands such as $\mathrm{CN^{-}}$. The $sp^{3}d^{2}$ and $d^{2}sp^{3}$ types give six-coordinate octahedral shapes, which need six ligands.
Final Answer:
The complex is tetrahedral with $sp^{3}$ hybridisation, option (A).
(A) $sp^{3}$
Quick Tip: Chloride is a weak field ligand, so Ni(II) with Cl forms a tetrahedral $sp^{3}$ complex.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation state of cobalt in $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}$ ?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
The oxidation state of the central metal equals the charge of the complex minus the total charge of the ligands.
Step 2: Calculation:
Let the oxidation state of Co be $x$. Ammonia is a neutral ligand (charge 0).
$$x + 6(0) = +3 \Rightarrow x = +3$$
Step 3: Check the Other Options:
$+5$ and $+4$ would give a complex charge of $+5$ or $+4$, and $+2$ would give $2+$. Only $+3$ matches the given $3+$. So (C) is correct.
Final Answer:
Cobalt is in the +3 state, option (C).
(C) $+3$
Quick Tip: Ammonia is neutral, so the metal carries the full charge of the complex.

questions.stem:
Identify reagent B in following reaction.
$\mathrm{R-X \xrightarrow{B} Nitroalkane}$
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
The nitrite ion, $\mathrm{NO_2^{-}}$, is an ambident nucleophile: it can attack through N or through O.
Step 2: Silver Nitrite:
$\mathrm{AgNO_2}$ is largely covalent, so the nitrogen lone pair is free for attack. The product is a nitroalkane, $\mathrm{R\text{-}NO_2}$.
$$\mathrm{R\text{-}X + AgNO_2 \rightarrow R\text{-}NO_2 + AgX}$$
Step 3: Check the Other Options:
$\mathrm{KNO_2}$ is ionic and attacks through oxygen, which gives alkyl nitrite $\mathrm{R\text{-}O\text{-}N{=}O}$. $\mathrm{NaOR}$ gives an ether and alcoholic KCN gives a nitrile. Option (A) is the reagent that gives the nitro compound. Option (A), $\mathrm{Ag\text{-}O\text{-}N{=}O}$, is the written form of silver nitrite.
Final Answer:
Silver nitrite gives the nitroalkane, option (A).
(A) $\mathrm{AgNO_2}$
Quick Tip: Silver nitrite ($\mathrm{AgNO_2}$) is covalent and attacks through nitrogen to give nitroalkane.

questions.stem: Which of the following $n$ mole compound is obtained when $2n$ moles of $\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl}$ treated of with $2n$ mole sodium atom in dry ether?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
When an aryl halide is heated with sodium metal in dry ether, two aryl groups join. This is the Fittig reaction.
Step 2: Balanced Reaction:
$$\mathrm{2\,C_6H_5Cl + 2\,Na \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} C_6H_5-C_6H_5 + 2\,NaCl}$$
So $2n$ mol of chlorobenzene and $2n$ mol of sodium give $n$ mol of biphenyl.
Step 3: Check the Other Options:
Benzene would form by reduction with a reagent such as Zn and acid. Phenol needs hydrolysis (aqueous NaOH at high temperature and pressure). Toluene needs methyl halide in the Wurtz-Fittig reaction, which is absent here. So (A) is correct.
Final Answer:
The product is biphenyl, option (A).
(A) Biphenyl
Quick Tip: Two aryl halides couple with sodium in dry ether to give biphenyl (Fittig reaction).

questions.stem: Which from the following compounds is not obtained when methyl bromide is treated with ethyl bromide in presence of sodium metal in dry ether?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
In the Wurtz reaction two alkyl groups join. With two different halides, three couplings are possible.
Step 2: Possible Couplings:
$\mathrm{CH_3 + CH_3}$ gives ethane.
$\mathrm{CH_3 + C_2H_5}$ gives propane.
$\mathrm{C_2H_5 + C_2H_5}$ gives n-butane.
Step 3: Check Option (D):
2-methylpropane, $\mathrm{CH_3CH(CH_3)_2}$, has a branched carbon skeleton. Joining methyl and ethyl groups can never create a branch, so it cannot be formed.
Step 4: Conclusion:
Ethane, propane and n-butane are all products. 2-methylpropane is not, so (D) is the answer.
Final Answer:
2-methylpropane cannot form, option (D).
(D) 2-methylpropane
Quick Tip: Cross Wurtz coupling gives three alkanes: propane, ethane, n-butane.

questions.stem: Which of the following pair of reagents is used for the conversion of carboxylic acid to alcohol ?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
A carboxylic acid is reduced to a primary alcohol, $\mathrm{RCOOH \rightarrow RCH_2OH}$. This needs a strong hydride donor.
Step 2: Standard Reagent:
Lithium aluminium hydride in dry ether, followed by hydrolysis with dilute acid, performs this reduction.
$$\mathrm{RCOOH \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4/H_3O^{+}} RCH_2OH}$$
Step 3: Check the Other Options:
$\mathrm{H_2/Ni}$ and $\mathrm{H_2/Pd}$ are catalytic hydrogenation reagents. They reduce C=C and C-C triple bonds easily but leave the carboxyl group untouched under ordinary conditions. The pair in (C), $\mathrm{B_2H_6/H_2O_2, OH^{-}}$, is the hydroboration-oxidation sequence normally written for converting alkenes into alcohols, and the textbook reagent for the acid-to-alcohol conversion is the hydride in (A).
Final Answer:
$\mathrm{LiAlH_4}$ followed by acid work-up is the standard reagent, option (A).
(A) $\mathrm{LiAlH_4/H_3O^{+}}$
Quick Tip: Lithium aluminium hydride followed by acidic work-up reduces RCOOH to a primary alcohol.

questions.stem: Which from the following hydroxy compounds contain only one $\mathrm{-OH}$ group in a molecule?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
Alcohols and phenols are classified as mono-, di- or trihydric by the number of $\mathrm{-OH}$ groups.
Step 2: Count the OH Groups:
Crotonyl (crotyl) alcohol: $\mathrm{CH_3CH=CHCH_2OH}$, one OH.
Ethylene glycol: $\mathrm{HOCH_2CH_2OH}$, two OH.
Pyrogallol: benzene-1,2,3-triol, three OH.
Hydroquinone: benzene-1,4-diol, two OH.
Step 3: Conclusion:
Only crotonyl alcohol is monohydric, so (A) is correct.
Final Answer:
Crotonyl alcohol has a single OH group, option (A).
(A) Crotonyl alcohol
Quick Tip: Count the OH groups: crotyl alcohol has one; glycol has two; pyrogallol has three; hydroquinone has two.

questions.stem: Identify the compound obtained when ethyl methyl ketone is treated with $\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}$ and hydrolyzed.
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
Grignard reagents add to the carbonyl carbon. Aldehydes (except HCHO) give secondary alcohols, and ketones give tertiary alcohols after hydrolysis.
Step 2: Reaction:
Ethyl methyl ketone is $\mathrm{CH_3COC_2H_5}$. The $\mathrm{CH_3^{-}}$ group of $\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}$ adds to the carbonyl carbon:
$$\mathrm{CH_3COC_2H_5 + CH_3MgBr \rightarrow C_2H_5C(CH_3)_2OMgBr \xrightarrow{H_2O} C_2H_5C(CH_3)_2OH}$$
The product is 2-methylbutan-2-ol.
Step 3: Check the Other Options:
(A) $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3COH}$ comes from acetone. (C) $\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_3COH}$ and (D) with two ethyl groups would need ethyl Grignard reagents. Only (B) has one ethyl and two methyl groups on the carbinol carbon.
Final Answer:
The product is 2-methylbutan-2-ol, option (B).
(B) $\mathrm{C_2H_5C(CH_3)_2OH}$
Quick Tip: A ketone with a Grignard reagent gives a tertiary alcohol after hydrolysis.

questions.stem: Which from the following is NOT a monocarboxylic acid?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
A monocarboxylic acid has exactly one $\mathrm{-COOH}$ group.
Step 2: Check the Options:
Toluic acid: methylbenzoic acid, one COOH.
Acrylic acid: $\mathrm{CH_2=CH\text{-}COOH}$, one COOH.
Phthalic acid: benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid, two COOH.
Isobutyric acid: $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH\text{-}COOH}$, one COOH.
Step 3: Conclusion:
Phthalic acid has two carboxyl groups, so it is a dicarboxylic acid and not a monocarboxylic acid.
Final Answer:
Phthalic acid is dicarboxylic, option (C).
(C) Phthalic acid
Quick Tip: Phthalic acid is benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid, with two COOH groups.

questions.stem: Which from following compounds is obtained when propionamide is treated with $\mathrm{Br_2}$ and concentrated aqueous KOH solution ?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
In Hofmann bromamide degradation, an amide reacts with $\mathrm{Br_2}$ and aqueous KOH to give a primary amine with one carbon atom fewer.
Step 2: Reaction:
$$\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CONH_2 + Br_2 + 4KOH \rightarrow CH_3CH_2NH_2 + 2KBr + K_2CO_3 + 2H_2O}$$
Propionamide has three carbons, so the amine has two: ethylamine.
Step 3: Check the Other Options:
(A) has four carbons, so it has more carbon than the amide. (B) is acetone, which has no nitrogen. (D) is ethyl bromide, which is not formed since nitrogen is retained. So (C) is correct.
Final Answer:
The product is ethylamine, option (C).
(C) $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}$
Quick Tip: Hofmann degradation removes one carbon atom as carbonate and gives a primary amine.

questions.stem: Which from following amines is obtained by Gabrial phthalimide synthesis?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
Gabriel phthalimide synthesis converts an alkyl halide into a primary amine through N-alkylphthalimide, followed by hydrolysis.
Step 2: Limits of the Method:
Aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution by phthalimide anion, so aromatic primary amines like aniline cannot be made this way. Also, only primary aliphatic amines can result, not secondary or tertiary.
Step 3: Check the Options:
(A) Aniline: aromatic amine, not possible.
(B) Ethylamine: primary aliphatic amine, possible from ethyl halide.
(C) Dimethylamine: secondary amine, not possible.
(D) $\mathrm{C_2H_5N(CH_3)_2}$: tertiary amine, not possible.
Step 4: Conclusion:
Only ethylamine can be prepared, so (B) is correct.
Final Answer:
Gabriel synthesis gives ethylamine, option (B).
(B) $\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}$
Quick Tip: Gabriel synthesis gives only primary aliphatic amines.

questions.stem: Which from following compounds is classified as oligosaccharide?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
Carbohydrates are classified by the number of simple sugar units they give on hydrolysis. Monosaccharides give none, and oligosaccharides give 2 to 10 units.
Step 2: Check the Options:
Ribose: a monosaccharide (aldopentose).
Sucrose: a disaccharide that gives glucose and fructose on hydrolysis, so it is an oligosaccharide.
Fructose: a monosaccharide (ketohexose).
Glucose: a monosaccharide (aldohexose).
Step 3: Conclusion:
Sucrose is the only oligosaccharide listed.
Final Answer:
Sucrose is an oligosaccharide, option (B).
(B) Sucrose
Quick Tip: Sucrose gives two monosaccharides on hydrolysis, so it is an oligosaccharide (disaccharide).

questions.stem: Which from following, sugar is an aldohexose?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
The name "aldohexose" means a sugar with an aldehyde group and six carbon atoms.
Step 2: Check the Options:
Ribose: aldehyde, five carbons, so aldopentose.
Fructose: ketone, six carbons, so ketohexose.
Lactose: a disaccharide, not a single sugar.
Glucose: aldehyde, six carbons, so aldohexose.
Step 3: Conclusion:
Glucose is the aldohexose.
Final Answer:
Glucose is an aldohexose, option (D).
(D) Glucose
Quick Tip: An aldohexose has six carbons and an aldehyde group; glucose fits.

questions.stem: Identify ureaformaldehyde resin from following polymers?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
Urea-formaldehyde resin is a condensation polymer formed from urea ($\mathrm{NH_2CONH_2}$) and formaldehyde (HCHO). The repeating unit contains $\mathrm{-NH\text{-}CO\text{-}NH\text{-}CH_2-}$.
Step 2: Check the Options:
Option (A) shows $\mathrm{-[CH_2-CH(CONH_2)]}_{n}\mathrm{-}$, which is polyacrylamide, an addition polymer of acrylamide.
Option (B) shows a chain with a phenyl group on every second carbon, which is polystyrene.
Option (C) is $\mathrm{[NH\text{-}CO\text{-}NH\text{-}CH_2]}_{n}$, the urea-formaldehyde repeating unit.
Option (D) is $\mathrm{[NH\text{-}(CH_2)_5\text{-}CO]}_{n}$, which is nylon-6.
Step 3: Conclusion:
Only option (C) matches the urea-formaldehyde resin.
Final Answer:
The repeat unit with urea and $\mathrm{CH_2}$ is option (C).
(C) $\mathrm{[NH\text{-}CO\text{-}NH\text{-}CH_2]}_{n}$
Quick Tip: Urea-formaldehyde resin repeats the unit $\mathrm{NH\text{-}CO\text{-}NH\text{-}CH_2}$.

questions.stem: Identify thermosetting polymer from following.
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
Thermosetting polymers are heavily cross-linked and become hard and infusible once heated and moulded. They cannot be remoulded.
Step 2: Check the Options:
Urea-formaldehyde resin: forms a cross-linked network, so it is thermosetting.
Polystyrene: linear chain, thermoplastic.
Buna-S: a synthetic rubber, an elastomer.
Terylene: a linear polyester, which is a fibre (thermoplastic).
Step 3: Conclusion:
Urea-formaldehyde resin is the thermosetting polymer.
Final Answer:
Urea-formaldehyde resin is thermosetting, option (A).
(A) Urea-formaldehyde resin
Quick Tip: Urea-formaldehyde resin is cross-linked and sets permanently on heating.

questions.stem: Identify antimicrobial compound from following.
questions.solution:
Step 1: Understanding the Concept:
Antimicrobials are substances that kill or stop the growth of microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi.
Step 2: Check Cinnamaldehyde:
Cinnamaldehyde is the main compound of cinnamon oil. It shows antimicrobial activity and is used as a natural preservative and flavouring, so it is the antimicrobial compound in the list.
Step 3: Other Options:
Curcumin is the yellow pigment of turmeric. Methyl salicylate is oil of wintergreen, used as a pain-relieving liniment (analgesic). Ascorbic acid is vitamin C, used as an antioxidant. These compounds are associated with other roles, so the item that matches the question is cinnamaldehyde.
Final Answer:
Cinnamaldehyde is the antimicrobial compound, option (C).
(C) Cinnamaldehyde
Quick Tip: Cinnamaldehyde from cinnamon oil has antimicrobial action.
